title: #63 Challenge Students to Think of a Correct Answer That No-One Else Will Think Of
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Barton describes his use of Learner-Generated Examples, a technique where students produce their own examples of a concept rather than simply solving pre-written questions, giving the teacher insight into the boundaries of their understanding. He focuses on one framework, "Give an Example of," originally a four-box grid prompting multiple examples plus "boundary examples" -- cases right at the edge of what does and doesn't satisfy a definition -- which reveal depth of understanding and surface misconceptions. He explains an early version of the grid confused students because the label "interesting" in one box was too vague, so he revised the wording to something clearer, which noticeably improved the quality of examples students generated. He also describes a peer-checking routine: students swap completed grids with a partner, who ticks examples they're confident are correctly placed and question-marks any they're unsure about, and the class then discusses the flagged, boundary-adjacent examples together.
points: Boundary examples -- cases right at the edge of a definition -- are more diagnostically useful than straightforward examples because they expose the limits of a student's understanding and surface misconceptions.

A poorly worded prompt ("interesting") produced confused, low-value student responses; rewording the box labels directly improved the quality of the examples generated, showing prompt design matters as much as the underlying technique.
The peer-checking step (partners marking each other's grids with ticks or question marks) turns example generation into a built-in formative assessment loop rather than a one-off task.
Discussing only the question-marked, boundary-adjacent examples as a whole class focuses limited lesson time on exactly the cases most likely to reveal genuine misunderstanding.
quotes: In my Tips for Teachers book, I describe three frameworks I use to enable students to generate their own examples, which gives me powerful insight into their understanding.
The bottom two boxes are designed to encourage students to generate boundary examples - in other words, examples right on the edge of what is and what is not true.
Boundary examples reveal the depth of a student’s understanding and can draw out key misconceptions.
The problem I found, however, was students did not know what the bottom-left box meant.
Once students have filled in all four boxes, I ask them to swap with their partner who then checks them.
We then discuss any examples labelled with a question mark as a class, as you can be sure these are the very examples right at the boundary of a concept and thus worthy of further investigation.
